```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
crowdkit_backend <- attribute_truth_backends()
crowdkit_available <- isTRUE(crowdkit_backend$available[crowdkit_backend$backend == "crowd_kit"])
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = crowdkit_available)
```

`vignette("truth-fusion")` covers `attribute_truth_fusion(method = "majority")`,
entirely in R, with no dependency beyond this package. This vignette covers
the *optional* second backend: `method = "dawid_skene"` and
`"one_coin_dawid_skene"`, via Python's `crowd-kit` through `reticulate`.
Nothing here is required to use the rest of the package.

```{r availability-note, eval = TRUE}
crowdkit_backend[crowdkit_backend$backend == "crowd_kit", ]
```

If `available` is `FALSE`, `attribute_truth_fusion(method = "dawid_skene", ...)`
errors with the exact reason (no Python found, or Python found but `crowdkit`
not installed) -- never a silent fall-back to `"majority"`. This package never
installs Python or any Python package on your behalf; the error message tells
you what to install yourself (`pip install crowd-kit`) and how to point
`reticulate` at it (`RETICULATE_PYTHON`, `reticulate::use_python()`, or a
Python already on `PATH`). The code in the rest of this vignette only
actually *runs* when `crowdkit_available` is `TRUE` above -- on a machine
without Python, you will still see every chunk, but not its output.

## A simulated physician active/inactive status example

Sixteen simulated NPIs, each with a true (simulated, known-to-us-but-not-to-
the-model) active/inactive status. Three sources report on each:

- `source_1` is highly reliable -- correct on 15 of 16.
- `source_2` is always correct.
- `source_3` always reports `"active"`, regardless of the true status: a
  pure false-positive-biased source (sensitivity 1, specificity 0) that
  carries no real discriminative information at all.

```{r simulate}
entities <- 1:16
true_status <- ifelse(entities %% 2 == 1, "active", "inactive")
claims <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(entities), function(i) {
  e <- entities[i]
  t <- true_status[i]
  source_1 <- if (e == 6) "active" else t # source_1's one error
  data.frame(
    entity_id = as.character(e), attribute = "status",
    source_id = c("source_1", "source_2", "source_3"),
    claimed_value = c(source_1, t, "active"), reference_year = 2024
  )
}))
```

```{r fit-ds}
ds_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "dawid_skene")
ds_result
```

Unlike `"majority"`, which votes independently within each entity-year,
Dawid-Skene fits *once*, jointly, across all 16 entity-years -- it estimates
one confusion matrix per source by pooling that source's evidence across
every entity it rated. `source_diagnostics` is where that shows up:

```{r source-diagnostics}
reliability <- unique(ds_result$source_diagnostics[c("source_id", "reliability_score")])
reliability[order(-reliability$reliability_score), ]
```

`source_3`'s `reliability_score` lands at exactly `0.5` -- chance -- correctly
identifying it as carrying no real information, not just "less reliable"
than the other two. Its full confusion matrix makes the reason explicit:

```{r source-3-matrix}
ds_result$source_diagnostics[ds_result$source_diagnostics$source_id == "source_3", ]
```

`error_probability` is `1` for reporting `"active"` regardless of whether the
true status is `"active"` or `"inactive"` -- `source_3` says the same thing
every time no matter what is actually true, which is exactly what a
false-positive-biased source looks like in a confusion matrix. (A source
that simply never reports a given label at all gets `error_probability = 0`
for every true label on that row, not a missing row -- `crowd-kit`'s own
output is sparse here, listing only label combinations a source actually
produced; leaving the gap would let a source that never discriminates look
reliable merely by never being scored on its missing cell.)

## Convergence is not accuracy

```{r entity-6}
ds_result$predictions[ds_result$predictions$entity_id == "6", ]
```

Entity 6 is `source_1`'s one error, and it is where the model gets the
*wrong* answer -- true status is `"inactive"`, but `dawid_skene` predicts
`"active"` with `model_score` over `0.9`, and `model_diagnostics$converged`
is `TRUE`. This is not a bug; it is exactly the kind of failure the model
cannot see from the inside. Once the fit comes to (wrongly) believe entity 6
is `"active"`, it also slightly discounts `source_2`'s correct `"inactive"`
report there as if it were one of `source_2`'s rare errors -- a
self-reinforcing loop between the latent-label estimate and the per-source
error estimates that EM has no way to escape once it locks in. A converged,
confident, successfully-executed fit is not evidence that the fit is
*right*. Treat `model_score` as `score_type = "posterior_probability"` says:
a probability under this model's own assumptions, estimated from this data,
never a validated probability of being correct.

## When sources share an upstream feed

The failure mode above is at least visible in principle -- a careful look at
`source_diagnostics` would flag `source_1` as imperfect. A more dangerous
version of the same problem is close to invisible: Dawid-Skene assumes every
source's errors are conditionally independent given the true label. Two
sources that are actually the same underlying data, copied -- a registry
mirrored into a second system, say -- violate that assumption completely,
and the model has no way to detect it from the claims table alone.

```{r copied-source-setup}
entities2 <- 1:12
true_state <- ifelse(entities2 %% 2 == 1, "CO", "NM")
error_entities <- c(2, 8) # nppes (and its copy) are wrong here
claims2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(entities2), function(i) {
  e <- entities2[i]
  t <- true_state[i]
  other <- if (t == "CO") "NM" else "CO"
  nppes_val <- if (e %in% error_entities) other else t
  data.frame(
    entity_id = as.character(e), attribute = "state",
    source_id = c("nppes", "pecos_copy", "op"),
    # pecos_copy is a VERBATIM copy of nppes -- same upstream feed, same errors
    claimed_value = c(nppes_val, nppes_val, t), reference_year = 2024
  )
}))
```

```{r copied-source-fit}
copied_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims2, method = "dawid_skene")
copied_result$predictions[copied_result$predictions$entity_id %in% c("2", "8"), ]
```

True state for entities 2 and 8 is `"NM"`; `dawid_skene` predicts `"CO"` for
both, and `model_score` rounds to exactly `1` -- not "highly confident," but
indistinguishable from certainty at four decimal places. `nppes` and
`pecos_copy` are not two corroborating sources -- they are one source's
claim, counted twice, outvoting `op`'s single correct report 2 to 1. The
model cannot tell that apart from two genuinely independent sources
agreeing, so its confidence is exactly as extreme as if they *were*
independent, for an answer that is wrong. If you suspect two sources might
share an upstream feed,
check that *before* trusting a confident Dawid-Skene fit:
`attribute_agreement()` and `attribute_source_corroboration()` (see
`vignette("consensus-and-corroboration")`) describe raw pairwise agreement
without this model's independence assumption, and are a reasonable first
place to look for a suspiciously perfect pair.

## `one_coin_dawid_skene`: one scalar per source, not a full confusion matrix

```{r one-coin}
oc_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "one_coin_dawid_skene")
oc_result$source_diagnostics[, c("source_id", "reliability_score")]
```

`"one_coin_dawid_skene"` simplifies each source to a single skill (its
overall probability of reporting correctly, not broken out by class), so
`true_label`/`observed_label`/`error_probability` are `NA` -- only
`reliability_score` is populated. It still ranks `source_3` lowest, but
cannot show *why* (a biased source and a merely-noisy source with the same
overall accuracy look identical to it); use `"dawid_skene"` when
distinguishing those matters.

## Diagnostics this backend adds

`model_diagnostics$converged` is `FALSE` (with a `warning()`, never silent)
if the EM loop used every one of `max_iterations` without its loss changing
by less than `convergence_tolerance`:

```{r nonconvergence, warning = TRUE}
attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "dawid_skene", max_iterations = 1L)$model_diagnostics[
  , c("converged", "n_iterations", "n_warnings")
]
```

`n_disconnected_components > 1` (also a `warning()`) means the worker-task
graph split into pieces sharing no evidence -- per-source reliabilities in
different pieces are not jointly identifiable from that one call. This can
be worse than just imprecise:

```{r disconnected, warning = TRUE}
disconnected_claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("1", "1", "2", "2"), attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
  claimed_value = c("CO", "CO", "NM", "NM"), reference_year = 2024
)
disconnected_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(disconnected_claims, method = "dawid_skene")
disconnected_result$model_diagnostics[, "n_disconnected_components"]
disconnected_result$predictions[, c("entity_id", "predicted_value", "abstained", "abstention_reason")]
```

Both entities abstain with `abstention_reason = "tied_vote"` -- even though
entity 1's two included sources (`a`, `b`) unanimously agreed on `"CO"`, and
entity 2's two sources unanimously agreed on `"NM"`. There is no real
disagreement on either task; `n_candidate_values` for both is `1`. With
nothing shared between the two components, Dawid-Skene has no evidence at
all to estimate any source's confusion matrix from, and falls back to a
flat prior across *every* candidate value seen anywhere in the call -- for
every task in the affected components, not just the ambiguous ones. A
flat prior over two values is, by construction, an exact tie. **Whenever
`n_disconnected_components > 1`, check an abstained prediction's
`candidate_scores$n_votes` before trusting the abstention** -- a task can
report "tied" here for a reason that has nothing to do with that task's
own evidence.

`on_source_conflict = "multi_value"` is rejected outright for this backend
(Dawid-Skene assumes one label per worker-task):

```{r multi-value-error, error = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "dawid_skene", on_source_conflict = "multi_value")
```

## What this does and doesn't establish

`"dawid_skene"`/`"one_coin_dawid_skene"` are a reliable, optional
*probabilistic* backend -- not yet a validated source of truth. They can
correctly identify a degenerate, uninformative source from its confusion
matrix alone (the first example above); they can also converge, with high
confidence, on a wrong answer when a source's rare error happens to align
with another source's bias (the second example), or when two sources share
an upstream feed the model has no way to see (the third). None of this is
checked against any real-world ground truth -- that is explicitly future
work (a held-out validation dataset, not yet built). Treat a confident
`model_score` the way you would treat a confident p-value from a model whose
assumptions you have not checked: as a reason to look closer at
`source_diagnostics` and at independent agreement checks, not as a
substitute for them.
